# Introduction to GitHub {#sec-introduction-to-github}

GitHub is a web-based service for hosting Git repositories. Simply put, you can host a remote repository on GitHub instead of hosting it locally on your computer or network. This makes it easy to access your repository from different computers and share it with others. However, GitHub is much more than a service for hosting repositories. It also provides a wide range of features that facilitate collaboration and can be used for many other purposes. Covering all these features would require an entire tutorial in itself, so in this chapter we will only introduce and illustrate a selection of GitHub's features.

GitHub has a web user interface that is easy to navigate and is often the most convenient way to interact with GitHub. However, explaining how to use the web interface in a written tutorial would require numerous screenshots and detailed instructions. Instead, in line with the philosophy of this tutorial, we will use the GitHub CLI to interact with GitHub from the command line. This works well for the features we will introduce, but keep in mind that the web interface may be more convenient for many tasks. You can find documentation on how to use GitHub, including its web interface, on the [GitHub website](https://docs.github.com/en).

It is important to understand that Git and GitHub are two different things. Git is a version control system, whereas GitHub is a web-based service for hosting Git repositories and facilitating collaboration. Similarly, the `git` and `gh` commands serve different purposes. We use `git` commands to perform Git operations, while we use `gh` commands to interact with GitHub through the GitHub CLI.


## Create a GitHub account and install the GitHub CLI

To do basically anything other than browsing and cloning repositories on GitHub, you need to create an account. You can create a free GitHub account by going to [https://github.com](https://github.com) and sign up.

As stated, we will interact with GitHub from the command line using the GitHub CLI. You can install it by running the following command:

<pre class="terminal">
$ winget install --id GitHub.cli
</pre>

This should work from Git Bash. If not, try running the command in PowerShell. Alternatively, download and install it from [https://cli.github.com/](https://cli.github.com/).

You need to restart your terminal before you can use the GitHub CLI `gh` commands.


## Authenticate with your GitHub account

The most technical aspect of using GitHub is to authenticate with your GitHub account. You need to do this to verify to GitHub that you are who you claim to be, so that you are allowed to access your GitHub account and push changes to your repositories etc. You can authenticate with your GitHub account from the command line using either HTTPS or SSH. It is outside the scope of this tutorial to go into any details about what this means, and to explain the pros and cons of each protocol. Here we will simply show how you can authenticate using HTTPS using the GitHub CLI. To authenticate with your GitHub account, run the following command:

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh auth login --git-protocol https --web --clipboard
</pre>

Follow the link given in the terminal. If you are not logged into your GitHub account already, you will be prompted to do so first. Then you will be asked to enter the one-time code that was provided in the terminal output (which should already be copied to the clipboard).

After doing this, use the following command to verify that authentication has succeeded. The output should look something like:

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh auth status
<span class="col-white">github.com</span>
  <span class="col-green">✓</span> Logged in to github.com account <span class="col-white">your-user-name</span> (keyring)
  - Active account: <span class="col-white">true</span>
  - Git operations protocol: <span class="col-white">https</span>
  - Token: <span class="col-white">gho_************************************</span>
  - Token scopes: <span class="col-white">'delete_repo', 'gist', 'read:org', 'repo', 'workflow'</span>

</pre>

After authentication, the GitHub CLI normally stores your credentials securely in Windows Credential Manager, so you do not need to authenticate every time you use GitHub. If secure credential storage is unavailable, the GitHub CLI will instead store your credentials in a plain text file.

The rest of this chapter assumes that you have created a GitHub account, and have authenticated with it to allow you to access and modify your repositories.


## Creating a repository on GitHub

There are two ways to get a repository on GitHub. You can either initialize a new project directly on GitHub, or you can upload a repository to GitHub from an existing local repository. If you are starting a new Git repository and you want to have a remote on GitHub, you have two choices: Initialize the repository on GitHub and clone it, or initialize the repository locally, and then upload it to GitHub. There is no right or wrong way to do this, it comes down to personal preferences.

You can initialize or upload a Git repository on GitHub using the `gh repo create [<name>] [flags]` command. You can find documentation on this command at [https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_repo_create](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_repo_create), or you can use `gh repo create --help` in the terminal. It is possible to create a repository interactively in the terminal by running `gh repo create` with no arguments, but that is not something we will explore here. Instead we will create repositories non-interactively, and in this case we need, as a minimum, to specify a name for the repository and use flags to specify if the repository is to be  public (`--public`) or private (`--private`). Public repositories can be seen by everyone, whereas private repositories can only been seen by yourself. 


### Initialize a new Git repository on GitHub

Let's illustrate how to initialize a new Git repository directly on GitHub. As mentioned before, besides giving the repository a name, we also need to to use a flag to specify whether the repository should be public or private. Furthermore, it is common practice to initialize a repository with an initial commit adding a README to the repository:

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh repo create init-on-github --public --add-readme
</pre>

This creates a new public repository called `init-on-github` in your GitHub account with an empty README file.

You can now clone the repository, automatically setting up the repository on GitHub as a remote, and start working on the project:

<pre class="terminal">
$ cd ~
$ git clone "https://github.com/your-user-name/init-on-github"
$ cd init-on-github
$ git log --oneline
<span class="col-hash">9caef1d</span> <span class="col-yellow">(</span><span class="col-head">HEAD </span><span class="col-yellow">-></span> <span class="col-branch-local">main</span><span class="col-yellow">,</span> <span class="col-branch-remote">origin/main</span><span class="col-yellow">,</span> <span class="col-branch-remote">origin/HEAD</span><span class="col-yellow">)</span> Initial commit
$ ls
README.md
$ git remote -v
origin  https://github.com/your-user-name/init-on-github (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/your-user-name/init-on-github (push)
</pre>


### Upload repository from existing local repository

Imagine you have the following Git repository set up locally:

<pre class="terminal">
$ mkdir ~/init-local-repo
$ cd ~/init-local-repo
$ git init
$ touch README.txt
$ git add README.txt
$ git commit -m"Initial commit"
</pre>

To upload the repository to GitHub, we can use `gh repo create` with the `--source` flag to specify a local repository to use as a source for the repository. Furthermore, we can use the `--push` flag to push the local commits to the GitHub repository, and use the `--remote` flag to specify the name for the remote:

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh repo create init-local-repo --public --source=. --remote=origin --push
$ git log --oneline
<span class="col-hash">f662630</span> <span class="col-yellow">(</span><span class="col-head">HEAD</span> <span class="col-yellow">-></span> <span class="col-branch-local">main</span><span class="col-yellow">,</span> <span class="col-branch-remote">origin/main</span><span class="col-yellow">)</span> Initial commit
$ git remote -v
origin  https://github.com/your-user-name/init-local-repo (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/your-user-name/init-local-repo (push)
</pre>


## Tools to facilitate collaboration

GitHub has a ton of features that are useful when collaborating on a project. Here we will briefly touch on some basic uses of some of these features.


### Issues

GitHub has a built-in issue tracking system that can be used to organize tasks, report bugs, request new features, and discuss work on a project. You can think of GitHub issues a collaborative to-do list or message board attached to a repository, allowing developers and users to discuss and organize work.

The GitHub CLI provides several commands for managing issues, which we will illustrate in the following example. For a complete list of commands and their options, see the [GitHub CLI documentation](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_issue)


#### Example 

Imagine we are working on a project with several collaborators. To illustrate how issues can be used to coordinate work, we first create a repository on GitHub and clone it locally:

<pre class="terminal">
$ cd ~
$ gh repo create issues-example --public --add-readme --clone
$ cd issues-example
</pre>

Suppose we want a new feature implemented in the project. We can create an issue describing the proposed feature using `gh issue create`:

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh issue create --title "Implement feature A" --body "Description of the feature to implement."
</pre>

GitHub assigns each issue a unique number within the repository. We can use `gh issue list` to list the issues in the repository:

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh issue list

<span style="color:grey"><u>ID</u>  <u>TITLE              </u>  <u>LABELS</u>  <u>UPDATED           </u></span>
<span class="col-bright-green">#1</span>  Implement feature A          <span style="color:grey">about 1 minute ago</span>

</pre>

We can see that the issue has been assigned the number 1. We can use this number to refer to the issue, for example when using `gh issue view` to inspect its contents:

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh issue view 1
</pre>

Other collaborators can now see the issue and discuss the proposed feature. For example, we can add a comment indicating that we will implement the feature:

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh issue comment 1 --body "I'll implement this feature."
</pre>

Once the feature has been implemented and the changes pushed to GitHub, we can close the issue using `gh issue close`:

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh issue close 1
</pre>

Finally, we clean up by deleting the example repository from GitHub and removing the clone:

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh repo delete issues-example --yes
$ cd
$ rm -rf issues-example
</pre>

If the GitHub CLI reports insufficient permissions to delete the repository, you may need to run `gh auth refresh -s delete_repo` and try again.


### Pull requests

A pull request is a GitHub feature that allows you to propose changes to a repository by requesting that changes from one branch be merged into another. Before the changes are merged, other collaborators can review the proposed changes, discuss them, and suggest improvements. Pull requests are therefore useful for coordinating and reviewing changes before they are integrated into a project.

For example, when developing a new feature in a separate branch, you can create a pull request to propose merging the feature into the main branch. This allows other collaborators to review the changes before they become part of the main version of the project.


### Forks

In some projects, not everyone has permission to push changes directly to the repository. This is particularly common in open-source projects, where anyone can contribute, but only certain people have write access to the repository.

GitHub addresses this through a feature called *forking*. A fork is a copy of a GitHub repository under your own account, linked to the original repository, which is called the *upstream repository*. Since you own the fork, you can make changes and push commits to it without affecting the original repository. You can then use a pull request to propose merging your changes into the upstream repository.

Forking is different from cloning a repository. While cloning creates a local copy of a repository on your computer, forking creates a separate repository on GitHub.


#### Example

Let's illustrate how forks and pull requests can be used together to contribute to a project where we do not have write access. Imagine that we want to contribute to the GitHub repository [github.com/thomas-rasmussen-alt/git-tutorial-fork-example](github.com/thomas-rasmussen-alt/git-tutorial-fork-example).

First we create a fork of the repository under our own GitHub account and clone it to our computer using `gh repo fork`:

<pre class="terminal">
$ cd
$ gh repo fork thomas-rasmussen-alt/git-tutorial-fork-example --clone
$ cd git-tutorial-fork-example
</pre>

Let's inspect the remote that have been configured in our local clone:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git remote -v
origin    https://github.com/your-user-name/git-tutorial-fork-example.git (fetch)
origin    https://github.com/your-user-name/git-tutorial-fork-example.git (push)
upstream  https://github.com/thomas-rasmussen-alt/git-tutorial-fork-example.git (fetch)
upstream  https://github.com/thomas-rasmussen-alt/git-tutorial-fork-example.git (push)
</pre>

We can se that two remotes have been configured automatically: `origin`, which points to our fork, and `upstream`, which points to the original repository. We can push changes to our fork through `origin`, but we do not have permission to push changes directly to the upstream repository.

Next, we create a feature branch, implement a change, and push the new branch to our fork:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git switch -c implement-feature
$ echo "Implementation of feature" > feature.txt
$ git add feature.txt
$ git commit -m "Implement feature"
$ git push -u origin implement-feature
</pre>

We can inspect the commit history to see how the branches now differ:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git log --oneline
$ git remote -v
origin    https://github.com/your-user-name/git-tutorial-fork-example.git (fetch)
origin    https://github.com/your-user-name/git-tutorial-fork-example.git (push)
upstream  https://github.com/thomas-rasmussen-alt/git-tutorial-fork-example.git (fetch)
upstream  https://github.com/thomas-rasmussen-alt/git-tutorial-fork-example.git (push)

We can see that two remotes have been configured automatically: origin, which points to our fork, and upstream, which points to the original repository. We can push changes to our fork through origin, but we do not have permission to push changes directly to the upstream repository.

Next, we create a feature branch, implement a change, and push the new branch to our fork:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git switch -c implement-feature
$ echo "Implementation of feature" > feature.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m "Implement feature"
$ git push -u origin implement-feature
</pre>

We can inspect the commit history to see how the branches now differ:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git log --oneline
d134f37 (HEAD -> implement-feature, origin/implement-feature) Implement feature
dd7b9d9 (origin/main, origin/HEAD, upstream/main, upstream/HEAD) Initial commit
</pre>

The new commit is not present in our feature branch and has been pushed to our fork on GitHub. However, the `main` branch in the upstream repository still points to the original commit. TODO: yes, but would it not also be important to emphasize that upstream is unchanged. Our changes have not altered the upstream repository, no commits and no branches have been added there.

We can now create a pull request proposing that our changes be merged into the `main` branch of the upstream repository:

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh pr create --repo thomas-rasmussen-alt/git-tutorial-fork-example --base main --head your-user-name:implement-feature --title "Implement feature" --body "Implementation of a new feature"
</pre>

TODO: in the above output, would it be better to omit the --body option? It does not add anything and the command is already really long?

Here, `--repo` specifies the upstream repository where the pull request should be created, `--base` specifies the branch we want to merge our changes into, and `--head` specifies the branch containing our proposed changes. Replace `your-user-name` with your GitHub username.

GitHub creates the pull request and displays its URL. We can inspect the pull request using `gh pr view`:

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh pr view
</pre>

The owner of the upstream repository can now review and discuss the proposed changes before deciding whether to merge them. We will not illustrate the review and merging process here.

Finally, we can clean up by closing the pull request, deleting our fork, and removing the local clone. Replace `<number>` with the number assigned to the pull request:

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh pr close &lt;number&gt; --repo thomas-rasmussen-alt/git-tutorial-fork-example
$ gh repo delete your-user-name/git-tutorial-fork-example --yes
$ cd
$ rm -rf git-tutorial-fork-example
</pre>


## GitHub pages

GitHub pages is a static site hosting service, that can take HTML, CSS, and Javascript files from a GitHub repository and turn them into a website. It is very simple to set up from a GitHub repository, and useful in a wide array of scenarios. Common use cases include:

- Documentation

- Personal websites

- Blogs

- Resumes


As an example, the tutorial you are currently reading is hosted as a static website on GitHub pages, based on the main branch of the repository that creates the tutorial. Every time the main branch is updated, the website is automatically updated!

It is outside the scope of this tutorial to go into details on how to use GitHub pages, but for more information see the official documentation at <a href="https://docs.github.com/en/pages">https://docs.github.com/en/pages</a>


## A note on licences

when making a Git repository publicly available on GitHub, it is important to consider how others are allowed to use its contents. If you put a repository on GitHub to share it with others, you should include a license that specifies what other people can do with your code. You are not obligated to include a license, but if you don't, default copyright laws apply, meaning that you retain all rights to your source code and no one may reproduce, distribute, or create derivative works from your work. This might not be what you want. GitHub strongly encourages you to include an open source licence, the MIT licence being a common choice. The MIT licence is a short permissive software license, that basically allows people to do whatever they want with your code, as long as they include the original copyright and licence in any copy of the code. Also, the licence states that you hold zero liability for use of the code. In many cases, this is a very reasonable license, and a good default choice. If you want to to learn more about licences, here are few resources that might be of interest:

[https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/licensing-a-repository](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/licensing-a-repository)

[https://opensource.guide/legal/#which-open-source-license-is-appropriate-for-my-project](https://opensource.guide/legal/#which-open-source-license-is-appropriate-for-my-project)

[https://choosealicense.com](https://choosealicense.com)

[https://www.tldrlegal.com](https://www.tldrlegal.com)


## Summary

In this chapter, we have introduced GitHub as a platform for hosting Git repositories and facilitate collaboration. We have learned how to create and manage repositories on GitHub, use issues to organize work, and use forks and pull requests to contribute to projects. We have also briefly introduced GitHub Pages and discussed the importance of licensing when sharing code.

Throughout the chapter, we have used the GitHub CLI to interact with GitHub from the command line. However, the web user interface is often more convenient for many tasks, particularly when browsing repositories and reviewing changes. Both interfaces have their advantages, and which one to use ultimately comes down to the task at hand and personal preferences.


## Exercises

### Exercise 1 - Managing GitHub repositories using the GitHub CLI

In this exercise we will practice using some of the GitHub CLI commands that have been introduced in this chapter to illustrate how a simplified workflow using GitHub might look like.

<b>Step 1 - Initialize a repository</b>

Initialize a public repository directly on GitHub with an initial commit adding a README and a MIT license to the repository. 

::: {.callout-tip title="Hint 1" collapse="true" icon="false"}

You can find the `gh repo create` documentation at [https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_repo_create](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_repo_create)

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Hint 2" collapse="true" icon="false"}

Use the `--license` flag to add a license. You can find a list of available licences by running `gh repo license list`.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh repo create my-repo --public --add-readme --license=mit
</pre>

:::


<b>Step 2 - Inspect repository</b>

Before we clone the repository, we want to inspect how it looks like. Unfortunately, there is no easy way to list files, or contents of files, in a GitHub repository in the terminal. Instead, we want to open the repository in the browser, so we can take a closer look at it. Do this by navigation to the repository using the web UI, or use the `gh repo view` command.

::: {.callout-tip title="Hint" collapse="true" icon="false"}

Use the `--help` flag to see the documentation for the `gh repo view` command.

:::


::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh repo view my-repo --web
</pre>

:::


<b>Step 3 - Clone the repository</b>

Make a local clone and `cd` into the repository. Afterwards look at the commit history and list the files in it.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ cd
$ git clone https://github.com/user-name/my-repo.git
$ cd my-repo
$ git log --oneline
5<span class="col-hash">f0b7da (</span><span class="col-head">HEAD</span> <span class="col-hash">-></span> <span class="col-branch-local">main</span><span class="col-hash">,</span> <span class="col-branch-remote">origin/main</span><span class="col-hash">,</span> <span class="col-branch-remote">origin/HEAD</span><span class="col-hash">)</span> Initial commit
$ ls
LICENSE  README.md
</pre>

:::


<b>Step 4- Push change to repository</b>

Commit a change in the main branch, and push it to the GitHub repository.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ echo "Add change" > file1.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"Add change"
$ git push
</pre>

:::


<b>Step 4 - Make an issue</b>

Make an issue to implement a feature. Besides adding a title and description of the issue, assign the issue to yourself and add a label.

::: {.callout-tip title="Hint" collapse="true" icon="false"}

Look at the `gh issue create` documentation at [https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_issue_create](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_issue_create), or use the `--help` flag in the terminal.

You can find a list of valid label values at [https://docs.github.com/en/issues/using-labels-and-milestones-to-track-work/managing-labels](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/using-labels-and-milestones-to-track-work/managing-labels).

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh issue create --title "Implement feature A" --body "Description of feature to be added" --assignee "@me" --label "enhancement"
</pre>

:::


<b>Step 5 - Add comment in issue</b>

Use `gh issue comment` to open the issue in the browser, and add a comment using the web UI. Start by using `gh issue list` to find the ID of the issue. 

::: {.callout-tip title="Hint" collapse="true" icon="false"}

Look at the documentation for the `gh issue comment`, using either the `--help` flag in the terminal, or by looking at the documentation at [https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_issue_comment](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_issue_comment)

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh issue list

Showing 1 of 1 open issue in user-name/my-repo

<span style="color:grey"><u>ID</u>  <u>TITLE              </u>  <u>LABELS     </u>  <u>UPDATED             </u></span>
<span class="col-bright-green">#1</span>  Implement feature A  enhancement  <span style="color:grey">about 51 minutes ago</span>

$ gh issue comment --web"
</pre>

:::


<b>Step 6 - Close issue</b>

Close the issue with the `gh issue close` command using a flag to specify the issue was closed because it was completed.

::: {.callout-tip title="Hint" collapse="true" icon="false"}

You can find the documentation for the `gh issue close` command at [https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_issue_close](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_issue_close), or you can use the `--help` flag to show the documentation in the terminal.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh issue close 1 --reason "completed"
</pre>
:::


<b>Step 7 - Clean up</b>

Delete the local clone and GitHub repository.

::: {.callout-tip title="Hint 1 - Deleting the repository" collapse="true" icon="false"}

Look at the documentation for the `gh issue` commands at [https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_issue](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_issue) or use `gh issue --help` to find a command that delete a GitHub repository.

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Hint 2 - Deleting the clone" collapse="true" icon="false"}

To delete the local clone use the `rm` command. Make sure to use appropriate flags to recursively delete all folders and files in the repository folder.

If you are uneasy about using the `rm`command (which is not unreasonable), just delete the folder manually.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh repo delete my-repo --yes
$ cd
$ rm my-repo -rf
</pre>

:::


### Exercise 2 - Contributing to an open-source project ###

TODO: rewrite exercise to use the fork repository used earlier, instead of the repository of the tutorial.

In this exercise we will practice forking a repository and making a pull request by contributing to an open-source project, namely the GitHub repository with the source code for this tutorial. The GitHub repository can be found at [https://github.com/thomas-rasmussen/git-tutorial](https://github.com/thomas-rasmussen/git-tutorial).

Find a spelling or grammar error in the source code^[All errors in the tutorial are on purpose for the sake of this exercise!], fix it, and make a pull request. Alternatively, if you are not familiar with websites built using Quarto, you can just make a random change.

<b>Step 1 - Fork and clone the repository</b>

Fork and clone the repository using either the web UI or the GitHub CLI.

::: {.callout-tip title="Hint" collapse="true" icon="false"}

You can fork a repository using the `gh repo fork` command. See [https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_repo_fork](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_repo_fork) for documentation on how to use the command. 

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

To fork and clone the repository at the same time using the GitHub CLI, use the following command:

<pre class="terminal">
<span># cd to an appropriate directory before forking and cloning the repository. Here we choose the home directory. </span>
$ cd
$ gh repo fork thomas-rasmussesn/git-tutorial  --clone
</pre>

:::


<b>Step 2 - Implement change</b>

Fix an error / implement a random change. Do this in a feature branch.

::: {.callout-tip title="Hint" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ cd git-tutorial
$ git switch -c pr-test
$ echo "Pull request test" > pr-test.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"Pull request test"
</pre>

:::

<b>Step 4 - Push changes to fork</b>

Push the changes to your fork of the original repository.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ git push origin pr-test
</pre>

:::

<b>Step 5 - Create pull request</b>

Create a pull request to merge the changes into the main branch of the original repository.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh pr create --title "PR test" --body "PR test"
</pre>

If someone else has already made a pull request with the title "PR test" this will nok work and Git will tell you so. In this case pick another title.

:::


<b>Step 6 - Cleanup (optional)</b>

Delete the fork and local clone now that you are done.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ gh repo delete git-tutorial --yes
$ cd
$ rm git-tutorial -rf
</pre>

:::
